articles.title: Everyone thinks they are cross-disciplinary (and maybe they are right)
articles.authors: Jessica Zier, Sijia Liu, Valerie Gruest, Nathan Walter
articles.abstract: Cross-disciplinary research has become both a promise and a puzzle for the field of communication—a discipline that celebrates boundary-crossing yet continually reflects on its unique contributions and distinct identity. Drawing on a survey of 278 editorial board members from leading communication journals, this study examines how a sample of researchers occupying key mentorship and gatekeeping roles conceptualize and practice cross-disciplinarity across academic lineages: their advisors, themselves, and their advisees. Results reveal widespread support for cross-disciplinary engagement, with most respondents describing their own work as bringing together ideas from different fields. However, further coding indicated that most scholars engage primarily in multidisciplinary rather than interdisciplinary or transdisciplinary forms of scholarship. Respondents viewed themselves and their advisees as more cross-disciplinary than communication scholars in general and their advisors, respectively, while also perceiving junior scholars, doctoral students, and funders as more supportive of cross-disciplinary work than journal editors and senior scholars. Qualitative findings further highlighted themes of disciplinary identity negotiation, institutional tensions, collaborative knowledge production, and the perceived importance of cross-disciplinary research for the field’s relevance and impact. Together, the findings portray a discipline that strongly values cross-disciplinary ideals while continuing to negotiate their meaning and implementation.

articles.title: From Resistance to Privilege: A narrative literature review on disconnection studies
articles.abstract: Over the past decade, academic research has shown a markedly increasing interest in the concept of digital disconnection, a phenomenon frequently conceptualized as the disconnection turn. Despite the various methodological and analytical approaches examined by previous literature reviews, the field still lacks a clear thematic framework and a disciplinary definition for the several practices of disconnection examined by this literature. This narrative literature review addresses the growing academic field of disconnection studies, seeking to map the main thematic areas that have emerged in the literature and the meanings attributed to them by scholars. Utilizing a mixed (qualitative-quantitative) methodological approach on a corpus comprising 432 contributions, the study identified seven thematic clusters. The analysis phase yielded a conceptual map of the core thematic areas within the literature, complemented by an explanation of the distribution of articles in the corpus across the three ERC (European Research Council) domains. The clusters are subsequently synthesized in a two-dimensional analytical framework. This framework distinguishes ‘Disconnection as Resistance’ from ‘Disconnection as Privilege’, while also highlighting the difference between disconnection as a ‘Performative act’ and disconnection as a ‘Collective issue’. The findings provide a theoretical framework for understanding the main conceptual approaches emerging in disconnection literature, while simultaneously offering a broader critical perspective of the structural factors that regulate disconnection practices in the age of platform society.

articles.title: Cinematic convergence and the 1990s: Games, Hollywood, and the formation of a digital media ecology
articles.abstract: In the 1990s, videogames were increasingly in dialogue with Hollywood cinema. Technological innovation accelerated videogames capacity to draw on the audio-visual language of cinema while the entertainment industries underwent corporate restructuring that favoured media conglomeration. As a result, videogames and films came to share aesthetic ambitions, industrial infrastructures, and the creative technologies that made new forms of entertainment possible. Significantly, it was an era when game studies started to evolve its own discourses, but these were frequently positioned in response to, or in conversation with, traditional screen—especially film—studies and the emerging studies of transmedia. This special issue revisits the 1990s as a period of extensive experimentation in which the cinematic and the ludic co-evolved within the material, industrial, and ideological conditions of a new era of digitally led global capitalism. Looking back on this pivotal decade with the benefit of hindsight, the collected articles offer fresh perspectives on the period, revealing also how the technological aspirations, aesthetic conventions, and corporate strategies that characterised the convergences of the 1990s continue to shape our understanding of videogames within the landscapes of the twenty-first century.

articles.title: (In)Visible politics: Influencers as brokers of the state on TikTok and Douyin
articles.abstract: Social media platforms are central to influencers’ pursuit of online visibility, yet little is known about how influencers strategically engage with the state across different political regimes to sustain that visibility. We examine how influencers on video-sharing platforms, many of whom originate in ostensibly non-political domains, navigate political crises as moments of intensified visibility, focusing on TikTok in Israel and Douyin in China. Drawing on a content analysis of 589 videos produced during Israel’s 2023 judicial reform and China’s 2020 COVID-19 crisis, we operationalize three visibility strategies: (1) state glamorization, (2) patriotic expression, and (3) out-group derogation as analytic lenses for examining how influencers broker the state within platform infrastructures. We show that influencers mobilize these strategies both proactively, by capitalizing on crisis-driven attention, and reactively, by aligning with dominant political narratives to avoid marginalization in saturated visibility environments. Across both cases, influencers operate as situational political brokers, translating state-linked discourse into platform-native vernaculars. We theorize political brokerage as a visibility practice emerging from transactional relations among influencers, platforms, and the state across democratic and authoritarian regimes, arguing that during moments of crisis, the state itself becomes a strategic visibility resource for influencers.

The narrative construction of disinformation: Reach and impact in Central and Eastern Europe
articles.authors: Dren Gërguri, Jaume Suau Martinez, Dinko Gruhonjić
articles.abstract: This study analyzes the reach and impact of disinformation narratives within four Central-Eastern Europe countries: the Czech Republic, Kosovo, Poland, and Serbia. Using survey data collected in mid-2023, we examine how citizens have been exposed to common disinformation narratives (reach) and how this prior exposure influences their belief in them (impact). The results provide empirical information on this underrepresented area, which highlights that the repeated, reinforcing impact of previous exposure is a universal cognitive mechanism. This study contributes to the literature in two significant ways. In theory, they demonstrate the value of shifting from a claim-based to a narrative-based paradigm, which is much more similar to the clustering, emotional appeal, and ideological framing of disinformation. The findings provide empirical evidence from an underrepresented region in the study of disinformation, demonstrating how foreign-sponsored and domestically produced narratives hijack all of those concerns and exploit existing political divisions, historical grievances, and media weaknesses.

articles.title: Whiteness and the ‘not-so-other’: Ukrainian refugees’ media self-representation in the UK
articles.abstract: This study examines the role of ‘whiteness’ in shaping the experiences of Ukrainian refugees in the UK, focusing on their self-representation on social media. The Ukrainian refugee crisis is portrayed in the media in ways that position Ukrainians as ‘like’ Europeans and as deserving of better treatment from host societies. Cultural proximity influences perceptions of refugees, who are often represented as the Other to Western modernity. Drawing on 50 Facebook posts and images, as well as interviews with 25 refugees living in temporary accommodation in the UK, the study finds that their online self-portrayals and reflections avoid the refugee label and show that they do not perceive themselves as refugees. The research demonstrates how Ukrainian refugees negotiate identity online in ways shaped by the media's power to frame whiteness and cultural proximity, rather than by conventional constructions of refugeehood, while still often aligning with distinctions and hierarchies evident in media portrayals of refugees.

Generative artificial intelligence adoption and employees' perspectives on AI at work: toward unalienated working life or AI-augmented alienation?
articles.abstract: Purpose Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is making its way into our working lives. Previous research has explored topics such as AI-related fears among working people and AI technology adoption in companies, but people's perceptions of AI in the context of AI adoption are still not well understood. This article looks at the intersection of AI technology adoption and AI-related job concerns in one company. Design/methodology/approach A rapid ethnographic case study of a Finnish energy company during its introduction of a generative AI tool was conducted. This article explores: (1) How is AI technology adoption managed? (2) How do employees perceive AI-related social risks concerning their working lives? And (3) how are perceived risks related to AI accommodated? We utilized Marx's framework on alienation to analyze employees' AI-related job concerns and future perceptions, and improvisational change management theory to analyze technology adoption strategy. Findings AI-related concerns included both job security-related and job quality-related concerns. AI-related fears also manifest in rhetorics on the alienation-reducing potential of AI and digital automation. Employees' initiative is emphasized in technology adoption, which underlines the importance of their AI acceptance. Originality/value The article illustrates how AI acceptance is constructed in work culture, and it also shows how a classic theory can be relevant for analyzing AI perceptions. It demonstrates why employees' AI acceptance is central in the context of employee-led practices in AI technology adoption.

articles.title: Organizational autopoiesis and digital platforms in industry – exploring the conditions of self-referential decision-making
articles.abstract: Purpose The study investigates how firms can stay in control of their business and advance new business ventures when using digital platforms. Conceptually, it draws on social systems theory to address business ventures through self-referential decision-making in its course as a foundation of systemic autopoiesis and organizational programs informing such decisions. Design/methodology/approach To understand organizational programs and self-referential decision-making in platform use, problem-centered interviews are conducted with experts from industry. Content analysis reveals patterns of self-referential decision-making regarding the use of digital platforms from which different types of programs can be deduced. Findings When using digital platforms, self-referential decision-making splits up into a part that occurs on platforms in daily usage and off platforms when preparing and interpreting the use of platforms to conduct business. From these findings, conclusions can be drawn about different dimensions of organizational programming, concerning (1) frequency and level of aggregation in data sharing, (2) signaling in negotiations, presenting a firm, e.g. as bold, aggressive or reliable, stable, (3) reliance on personal ties and networks outside beyond the business activities address on the platform and (4) the direction of fit of platform data being either a descriptive approximation of business or a prescription for collaboration. Originality/value The study draws attention to autopoietic dynamics in business ecosystems that are essential for creative evolution driving economic development. It establishes a new approach to digital platforms through the lens of social systems theory with implications for theory development and the practice of platform design and operation.

articles.title: Antecedents and impact of distrust of generative AI in organizations: a socio-psychological perspective
articles.authors: Junjun Li, Xinyue Chen, Tangfa Chen
articles.abstract: Purpose As organizations increasingly adopt generative artificial intelligence (GAI) to enhance productivity, growing worker distrust may hinder this progress. While there is emerging literature from a technology acceptance perspective, the factors driving distrust from a socio-psychological perspective and the impact of distrust on adoption intentions require deeper exploration. We developed and validated a comprehensive framework to examine GAI distrust within organizations by integrating social cognitive theory and nudge theory. The framework identified pro-social nudges, outcome expectations, security concerns and privacy self-efficacy as key antecedents of distrust and assessed how distrust affects adoption intentions. Design/methodology/approach A survey of 1,005 active workers was conducted in China. The data were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling and the PROCESS macro for SPSS (Model 4). Findings While pro-social nudges and security concerns increased distrust, they did not directly affect adoption intentions. In contrast, positive outcome expectations and privacy self-efficacy reduced distrust and enhanced adoption intentions. The mediating and suppression effects of distrust were also discussed. Originality/value This study offers a novel framework for understanding the antecedents and impact of GAI distrust, providing practical insights for organizations and GAI developers to mitigate distrust within a broader social-psychological context.

articles.title: “Human-like or cartoon-like?” The impact of virtual influencer style on consumer forgiveness propensity following service failures
articles.authors: Yizhi Liu, Ying Luo, Yu Liu, Meixing Li
articles.abstract: Purpose Virtual influencers have increasingly become a critical force in shaping consumer behavior. Accordingly, an in-depth examination of consumers’ response mechanisms following service failures by virtual influencers has emerged as an important research topic within the virtual influencer literature. Design/methodology/approach Using virtual influencer service failures as the research scenario, three experiments were conducted to examine consumers’ forgiveness propensity following service failures involving different types of virtual influencers. Findings The results of the three experiments show that, in service failure situations, compared with anthropomorphic virtual influencers, cartoon-like virtual influencers induce a higher level of consumer forgiveness propensity. This effect is mediated by responsibility attribution. Anthropomorphic virtual influencers are perceived as bearing greater responsibility because of their more salient human-like characteristics, which in turn, reduce consumers’ forgiveness propensity. The presence or absence of an algorithmic explanation affects consumers’ responsibility attribution for service failures, and uncanny perception negatively affects forgiveness propensity. Research limitations/implications This study focuses on recommendation failures and value-based failures and uses samples drawn from a specific cultural context. Future research could examine additional types of service failure, explore cross-cultural differences, and investigate dynamic service recovery processes over time. Practical implications The findings provide guidance for firms in selecting appropriate virtual influencer designs, managing algorithmic transparency, and developing effective service recovery strategies. Organizations should carefully balance anthropomorphic design and perceived uncanniness while tailoring communication strategies following service failures. Originality/value This study expands theoretical research on human–computer interaction and human-computer collaboration in the field of AI service marketing, while also providing practical insights for enterprises seeking to effectively optimize the remedial measures for virtual influencer service failures.

articles.title: Modality matters: comparing the persuasiveness of text- and voice-based conversational agents and non-interactive messages in health communication
articles.authors: Ziyang Gong, Junqi Shao, Nisa Rahman, Leona Yi-Fan Su, Yi-Cheng Wang
articles.abstract: Purpose Text- and voice-based conversational agents (CAs) provide interactivity beyond the messages public health agencies traditionally use to share information and correct misperceptions. Yet, little research has compared how interactivity and modality influence misperception correction and behavior change. This study examines how modality and information quantity shape cognitive load, misperception change, and behavioral intention. Design/methodology/approach A 3 (modality: non-interactive message vs. text-based CA vs. voice-based CA) × 2 (information quantity: short vs. long) between-subjects experiment was conducted with 1,157 U.S. adults. Findings Both CA modalities were associated with lower post-intervention misperceptions than non-interactive messages. Relative to text-based CAs, voice delivery was linked to higher cognitive load, which in turn was associated with greater post-intervention misperceptions and lower intention to adopt healthy behavior. Nevertheless, when information quantity, cognitive load, preexisting and post-intervention misperceptions, and preexisting behavioral intention were controlled for, voice-based CAs were directly associated with the intention to adopt recommended behaviors. Information quantity did not moderate the relationship between modality and cognitive load. Originality/value To our knowledge, this study is the first controlled experiment to compare text-based CAs, voice-based CAs, and social media messages used to correct health misinformation, while clarifying the mechanisms through which they shape behavior change. The results show that neither CA modality is consistently more effective than the other across all outcomes. As such, practitioners should adopt a “fit-for-purpose” strategy, i.e. use text-based CAs when demands for comprehension are high and voice-based CAs when the main goal is to motivate behavior change.

Trust Formation in AI Expert Systems
articles.abstract: Abstract: As artificial intelligence expert systems (AIES) are increasingly used in domains such as medicine, psychotherapy, law, finance, and education, it remains important to understand what shapes their perceived trustworthiness relative to human experts. A central limitation of prior research is that findings are often difficult to generalize across domains because domain and stakes are rarely varied together within the same design. We address this issue in a preregistered online vignette experiment in which UK participants ( N = 898) evaluated advice from an AIES and a human expert under low- and high-stakes conditions in one of five domains. Across all domains and both stake levels, human experts were perceived as more trustworthy than AIES, whereas AIES were perceived as riskier. For trustworthiness, between-domain effects were significant but small on average, mainly affecting the size of the human–AIES difference, which was largest in medicine and psychotherapy and smallest in education. For perceived risk, stakes played a larger role than domain, with high-stakes situations increasing perceived risk across domains. Importantly, trustworthiness and perceived risk did not change in parallel across conditions: Domain differences were comparatively small for trustworthiness, whereas stakes played a larger role in perceived risk. Overall, the findings suggest that cross-domain differences are smaller than often assumed once stakes are controlled, and that stakes matter more than domain for understanding perceived risk when people evaluate AIES advice.

articles.title: Person-Centered Support From Chatbots Versus Humans
articles.authors: Siyue Li, Runnan Wei, Shiyu Han, Mengwei Dang
articles.abstract: Abstract: This study aims to examine whether and how perceived identity of a support provider and message quality would affect perceived agency of the provider and support outcomes. A total of 196 college students in China participated in a laboratory experiment. Each participant was instructed to discuss a personal problem with either a chatbot or a human who would provide higher or lower person-centered support as preprogrammed. The results showed that perceived identity of a support provider and person-centeredness of support messages jointly affected participants’ perceptions of the provider agency, which in turn positively influenced participants’ emotional distress reduction, reappraisal, and perceived validation. The findings provide theoretical and pragmatic implications for the application of human–computer interaction in supportive communication.

articles.title: Extending Relational Turbulence Theory by Examining the Experiences of Latina/o/x/e Couples Facing Migration-Based Family Separation
articles.authors: Kyungin Kim, Jennifer A. Kam, Karla Vazquez, Ricardo Delgado Solis, Andrew C. High
articles.abstract: This study tested a portion of relational turbulence theory with 58 highly under-resourced Latina/o/x/e couples navigating migration-based family separation (i.e., where one partner migrated to the United States, while the other remained in a Latin American country, most often with their children). Couples completed pre- and post-conversation surveys and participated in an audio-recorded phone conversation discussing their experiences. Actor-partner interdependence mediation models (APIMeM) showed that pre-conversation self and partner uncertainty were positively related to post-conversation perceived partner disconnection (biased cognitive appraisals), which in turn was related to less openness about separation stress (communicative engagement) for partners in Latin America. Further, partner and relationship uncertainty of U.S.-based partners were indirectly related to less openness among partners in Latin America, highlighting the interdependent nature of partners’ relational experiences. Familismo only moderated one of the tested associations. Findings extend RTT’s applicability to this structurally and culturally distinct context and point to the urgency of providing stratified support for families facing systemically driven relational stress.

articles.title: How the Cold War Broke the News: The Surprising Roots of Journalism’s Decline
Science Journalism on Controversial Fields: Contextualizing Audience Expectations and (Dis)Approval of the Watchdog Role
articles.abstract: Journalism research differentiates between various conceptions of roles and societal functions that journalism is expected to perform. Previous research has mainly examined journalists’ role perceptions, while audience views remain underexplored. However, in the context of science journalism on controversial scientific fields such as climate change or Covid-19, audience insights are particularly relevant given that media coverage may shape public perceptions of science and influence crisis responses. This study combines semi-structured interviews and focus group discussions to investigate what functions audiences expect from science journalism on controversial scientific fields, focusing on context-dependent (dis)approval of the watchdog role. Findings indicate that audiences expect science journalism to fulfill both traditional and science- or crisis-specific functions. Regarding the watchdog role, participants emphasized journalists’ task of uncovering misconduct and scientific norm violations in research underlying policy decisions. However, participants also viewed watchdog journalism as a balancing act as there are many forms of inappropriate critical reporting that might foster distrust in science and media. The findings are discussed regarding their implications for journalism practice and the role of watchdog science journalism in shaping public perceptions of controversial science.

articles.title: Piloting the Integration of AI-Driven Detection Methods to Counter Disinformation in Organizational Processes
articles.abstract: With the rise of generative AI, the increasing threat of automatically generated uncivil content (including misinformation for information warfare up to cyber-bullying purposes) makes the protection of open online discourse even more pressing than before. In the implementation of measures for countering these threats, the different intervention objectives of stakeholders, their workflows, and IT support need to be considered. Stakeholders include online social network moderators, journalists, fact-checkers, social listeners, as well as authorities and organizations with safety- and security-related tasks. Given the sheer volume of online social network content, automated or community-based solutions are required to detect (automated) misinformation. However, detection solutions are predominantly message-focused and target end-users, leaving experts without systematic, large-scale perspectives on coordinated disinformation campaigns to guide countermeasures. To bridge this gap, we conduct an expert-centered study on the integration of detection methods proposed by the research community. Our contributions are threefold: (a) We adopt disinformation features from a previous study and draw connections to literature on detection methods; (b) semi-structured interviews yield vignettes that expose the spectrum of goals, constraints, tools, and decision-making processes employed by experts, informing requirements for method integration; (c) we design a demonstrator that showcases representative methods to uncover unexplored concepts, probe affordances and limitations in context, and evaluate conceptual fit during the interviews. Together, these steps bridge the gap between data- and AI-driven detection techniques from research and the practical needs of diverse stakeholders confronting targeted and large-scale disinformation.

articles.title: Platformed Care: Gender and Care Mobilities Across Ride-Hailing Platforms
articles.authors: Mónica Humeres, Catalina Alarcón, Jacqueline Vega-Poblete
articles.abstract: This article examines how ride-hailing platforms mediate care mobility in everyday contexts, focusing on women-only and mixed-gender services in Chile. Drawing on 37 qualitative interviews with users and drivers, the study shows that caregiving responsibilities are an important yet underexamined reason women engage with these platforms, highlighting the gendered organization of care-related mobility. Participants use apps to coordinate children's routines, assist elderly relatives, and manage everyday travel with limited time, resources, and support. The findings show that these practices extend beyond transport. Women drivers often perform additional unremunerated forms of care, including waiting beyond scheduled times, offering emotional support, and assisting dependents. These interactions reveal how platform-mediated mobility operates across blurred boundaries between paid service and informal care, shaped by gendered expectations around responsibility and care. The article introduces the concept of platformed care to describe how mobile media and mobility platforms are used to coordinate and delegate caregiving-related mobility under conditions of distance and gendered vulnerability. Rather than resolve structural constraints, these platforms reorganize care mobility while reproducing existing inequalities.

articles.title: Free Smartphones? But Still Finding It Difficult to Find Place for Phones in Their Lives: Understanding Digital Interactions of Older Widow Women in Rural India
articles.abstract: This study is an exploration of the digital interactions of older widowed women living in rural India, who received free smartphones under a government scheme aimed at empowering marginalized women. Situated within the intersectionality framework, the research is an analysis of how the interplay of age, gender, widowhood, and rural residence shapes these women’s experiences with technology. Based on semistructured interviews with 16 widowed women aged 60–85 years, it was found in the study that the majority of the respondents are not using the smartphones themselves but have passed on the smartphones to younger female family members, citing utility to younger members and sociocultural norms. The study highlights the complex dynamics of digital inclusion in the Global South, where sociocultural factors lead to expectations that women conform to stereotypes about gender, age, and social status (being widowed) and, hence, significantly influence the adoption and use of technology. The study underscores the need for customized digital literacy initiatives that address both technical skills and the cultural stigmas surrounding technology use among older women living in rural areas. The study contributes to the discourse on the digital divide by focusing on a group that embodies several marginalities, offering insights for policy frameworks aimed at equitable digital empowerment.

articles.title: Aspirational technologies of the (disabled) self: Confessional, self-examinatory, and ascetic masculinities among food delivery riders on China’s digital platforms
articles.abstract: Digital platforms are increasingly offering new employment and social participation opportunities for people with disabilities (PWDs). This study examines the intersections of digital platforms, disability, and masculinity in China. Drawing on in-depth interviews and ethnography with 12 disabled male food delivery riders, it explores how platform-based delivery work serves as a site to negotiate masculinity and social recognition. The findings indicate that platforms not only offer relatively accessible and flexible income opportunities, enabling participants to engage in socially valued work and gendered responsibility, but also mobilize aspirational discourses that promise future inclusion and moral recognition while demanding intensified temporal discipline, bodily endurance, and the willingness to “eat bitterness.” Thus, digital platforms constitute an ambivalent space where inclusion and constraint coexist, enabling gendered self-formation while introducing new forms of discipline. Ultimately, this study calls for greater attention to the challenges faced by PWDs in digital labor.

articles.title: Learning the algorithm: Responsibilization and the limits of agency on YouTube
articles.abstract: Content creators invest extensive effort in “learning the algorithm” to secure visibility and growth. While existing research documents the proliferation of folk theories and optimization strategies, less attention has been paid to the structural conditions under which such learning unfolds. Drawing on a computational analysis of 179 YouTube videos discussing the platform’s algorithm, this article identifies recurring interpretive patterns that frame visibility as optimizable through metrics, strategic adjustment, and disciplined self-management. This paper argues that attempts at algorithmic learning are sustained by an asymmetry between epistemic agency – the capacity to interpret metrics and hypothesize about system behavior, and effective agency – the capacity to reliably influence outcomes. Because large-scale machine-learning systems are probabilistic, multi-objective, and continuously recalibrated, effective control remains systemically indeterminate. This asymmetry produces governance through responsibilization: creators internalize responsibility for unstable outcomes, sustaining engagement because the system appears responsive while remaining structurally uncontrollable.

articles.title: Overconfident youth, underconfident elders: Age differences in algorithmic knowledge confidence and information perceptions
articles.abstract: Age-related differences in algorithmic knowledge are typically interpreted as competence gaps that render younger “digital natives” better equipped and older users more vulnerable in algorithmically curated environments. This study challenges these assumptions by examining (a) algorithmic knowledge confidence—whether users’ subjective algorithmic knowledge exceeds or falls short of their algorithmic awareness and knowledge—and (b) what consequences such misalignment has for information environment perceptions. Using US survey data ( N = 1205), this study found systematic misalignment between subjective and awareness-based algorithmic knowledge: younger users overestimate their understanding, whereas older users underestimate theirs. Social media use partially mediated the age–knowledge confidence relationship. Knowledge confidence, in turn, predicted perceived information reliability and diversity. These findings reveal that critical assessment of information environment is determined not by knowledge level alone but by alignment between subjective and awareness-based knowledge, highlighting the need for age-tailored interventions addressing knowledge overconfidence and underconfidence.

articles.title: Social Media and the Smart City: A Systematic Review of City- and Citizen-Led Digital Spaces
articles.abstract: This systematic review examines how social media is conceptualized and studied within the context of smart cities, with a particular focus on the distinction between city-led and citizen-led digital spaces. Analyzing a sample of 50 peer-reviewed articles, the review identifies dominant techno-functionalist approaches that frame social media primarily as a data source for urban optimization, event detection, and service delivery. While some studies gesture toward participatory or socially embedded uses of social media, the majority lack engagement with specific urban contexts or active representations of cities and their citizens. The review highlights a significant gap in research on the actually existing smart city and the sociocultural dimensions of urban digital life. The findings underscore the need for future research to move beyond top-down, efficiency-driven narratives and to critically engage with emerging technologies, such as generative artificial intelligence, in both institutional and grassroots urban media practices. The article calls for a reimagining of smart cities and smart citizenship that centers participatory and socially grounded perspectives.

articles.title: “You Might Like Each Other”: Mass Customization and the Structuring of Sociality Among Chinese Generation Z on the Soul App
articles.authors: Shuyao Zhao, Linxin Wang, Yao Dai
articles.abstract: We employed the framework of mass customization to investigate how the Soul app, a leading interest-based social platform, is reshaping sociality among Chinese Generation Z. Six months of participatory observation, from December 2024 to June 2025, in Soul’s interest-driven communities and semi-structured interviews with 11 users aged 21–29 served to explore how algorithmic mechanisms, personality tests and tag-based systems facilitate interest-driven connections. The findings reveal that Soul’s design fosters emotional support and fluid self-presentation through virtual identities yet simultaneously reinforces cultural and economic stratification by creating exclusive circles and algorithmic social cocoons. Members of Generation Z actively negotiate these constraints by deploying emotional strategies and identity adjustments to balance authenticity with platform logics. By examining algorithmic matching as an instance of mass customization in shaping sociality, this study advances the understanding of how digital natives in China navigate the tensions between personalization, scalability, and inequality in online interactions. The research contributes to platform studies by highlighting the dual role of algorithmic infrastructures as both enablers of individualized sociality and mediators of digital stratification in an individualized digital era.
